about: Strategy claims extracted from community hero guides. Each claim quotes its source. General principles are claims made independently by several guides. Pilot run over four guides; not yet the full set.

fields.scope: general: holds across heroes. hero: specific to one hero's cards.
fields.status: current: matches data/cards.json. stale: the guide predates the second printing and the card it relies on has changed. unchecked: not compared yet.
fields.engine: testable-now: the engine can measure it with a bot variant today. needs-card-text: depends on card effects the engine does not apply yet. needs-opponent-model: depends on bots that read and react to each other.

principles.claim: Wound a hero early in the round, then finish them on turn 4, when their hand is nearly empty.
principles.reason: Every hero holds only five cards. Each defense spent earlier leaves fewer answers later, so even durable heroes fall to a late follow-up.

evidence.quote: someone from your team hits a target with a discard and wounds them, and then on turn 4 someone hits them again
Even the tankiest of heroes are very vulnerable to this strategy, because everyone has 5 cards.
its most common use is eliminating wounded opponents on turn 4 by going faster than whatever they play

principles.test: Brawler variant that, among attack targets, prefers the enemy hero with the fewest cards in hand. Compare kills and win rate against the plain Brawler.

principles.claim: Keep defense cards in hand to block with, instead of playing them for their action.
principles.reason: A defense card's value is the threat it answers. Played early, it no longer protects you later in the round.

evidence.quote: The best use for this card is often holding it in your hand and using them like block cards.
holding that card in your hand until the right moment is the key to getting the most out of this hero
they played their defense cards earlier in the round, they "let their shields down" and got punished for it

principles.test: Brawler variant that plays its highest-defense card last in the round. Compare deaths per game against the plain Brawler.

principles.claim: Playing a low-initiative card can be an advantage: you act after seeing what everyone else did.
principles.reason: Initiative orders actions. The last to act reacts to resolved moves instead of guessing them.

evidence.quote: The slow initiative means you get to see what everyone else does, then make the best decision with that information.
At 2/1/1 initiative you’re green cards are the slowest in the game (This is a good thing)
you can go slow (7 or 8 INI), defend the minions from the faster enemy attacks, and then rocket off to get your own minion

principles.test: Only measurable once a bot chooses its action from the board state after others have moved. The current Brawler gains nothing from acting late.

principles.claim: To finish a wounded hero, you must act before their defense or escape. Buy initiative for it.
principles.reason: A wounded hero escapes or blocks on their own turn. A faster attack lands before that turn comes.

evidence.quote: Purchase lots of INI and a Range item for maximum effect.
It can require some initiative items to go faster than opponents' blues
dash through an enemy hero to start or (more likely) finish a fight before they can do anything to stop you

principles.test: Bot variant whose level-up choice favours initiative items. Compare kills against a variant that favours attack items.

principles.claim: Threaten an enemy so they must choose between taking a minion and staying safe. Either answer is a gain for you.
principles.reason: If they stay, you get a kill or coins. If they run, you get the minion and they do not.

evidence.quote: you can often put them in a position of choosing between defeating a minion, or running for their lives. If they don't run, lots of coins for you. If they do run, well you get a minion and they don't, win win!
using her silver to jump to squishy opponents to force them out of minion takes
Make sure that they are giving up something (e.g. position and/or farm) if they do that.

principles.claim: A telegraphed play invites a counter. Setting up a threat also reveals it.
principles.reason: Opponents see your position and resolved cards. A play only one card can make is a play they can block.

evidence.quote: moving into position is a big tell that this card is coming
the dash on this card is predictable and clever enemies will threaten your landing point
you are predictable and a clever enemy will move in to threaten you on the turn you wish to repeat your red

principles.claim: Being in the battle zone at the end of the round, and denying enemy minion kills, wins games more reliably than kills do.
principles.reason: Minion battle pushes the wave, and minion kills give coins. Denying a minion kill denies both.

evidence.quote: Be in the battlezone at the end of each round and you will have a VERY hard time losing the game.
to not only stop the enemy team from pushing the wave, but ALSO stop them from collecting coins
threatening oneshots in order to maintain wave pressure can be a primary strategy for her, since she often wants to take the final wave victory

principles.test: Bot variant that, on turn 4, moves into the battle zone rather than chasing the nearest enemy. Compare wins by push against the plain Brawler.

principles.claim: Fast, mobile heroes are best threatened by ranged attacks, not by chasing them.
principles.reason: A melee hero cannot keep pace with high movement and initiative. Range reaches without catching up.

evidence.quote: Heroes can’t really keep pace with Tigerclaws premium movement and initiative. The only way they can consistently threaten him is with ranged attacks.

principles.note: One source only. Needs confirmation from other guides before it counts as general.

principles.claim: Cards that heal allies but not yourself underperform, because enemies kill the healer first.

evidence.quote: The problem is that when people see that you can heal others, they simply target you instead.

principles.note: One source, and Rowenna's guide values ally healing highly. A disagreement worth checking in more guides.

principles.claim: A ranged hero who stays on the fringe leaves their teammate open to being outnumbered.

evidence.quote: beware 'cause leaving your teammate alone like that risks them getting ganged up on while you are away

principles.claim: Play the minion-saving green from the first turn of the game to stop the enemy push.

evidence.quote: Use this card (Even on the first turn of the game!)

principles.note: Second printing (Shield, Bolster, Fortify) costs a silver or basic card per save, not any card. The trade-off has changed.

principles.claim: The alternate red, not the charge, is Brogan's real kill threat. The charge is mostly for crossing the map and for bluffing.

evidence.quote: This is the actual killer. Any target that gets wounded will have a hard time escaping this card
Sometimes you can bluff by setting up this card but choosing a different one, just the threat of this can really junk up an enemies round.

principles.claim: Play silver for immunity, then attack next turn without fear of retaliation.

evidence.quote: it allows you to attack the turn after you play silver. Play this on the turn you’re immune allows you to attack heroes or minions without fear of retaliation

principles.note: Second-printing silver (Blend Into Shadows) needs adjacent terrain and is initiative 6. The combo may still hold but with a positioning condition.

principles.claim: Upgrade into the coin-stealing green first. Taking enemy coins slows their levels while speeding yours.

evidence.quote: You can get enemy heroes seriously behind by removing the coins, and get seriously ahead at the same time.

principles.note: Second printing takes 1 or 2 coins instead of removing 2 and gaining 2. The coin-swing idea survives, its size does not.

principles.claim: Rowenna initiates and protects, but needs a teammate who can close kills.
principles.reason: Her gold lets the target retrieve a card before the attack, so it rarely finishes a wounded hero.

evidence.quote: Rowenna is more of a support character than she looks, and requires support in return to shine.
This prevents her from using this to finish off a wounded enemy

principles.claim: Against Rowenna, predict her silver and move out of its range. Without it she has little movement for the round.

evidence.quote: if you can predict when this will be and get out of range, she is forced to hold and get no movement leaving her mostly out of the round

principles.claim: Swift's second attack comes from sequencing red into the gold reload, so the red's slot position matters.

evidence.quote: Because sequencing red into gold is your only way of getting two attacks in a round you are predictable

principles.note: Second-printing Reload! repeats the rightmost resolved card, not the previous turn slot, and gained a minion-defeat option. Most of the guide's sequencing advice needs rereading against the new deck.

principles.claim: Against Nebkher, leave the sniper red: he can copy the shot back.

evidence.quote: Against a NebKher you will switch out of this 95% of the time.
